stem: A 9-year-old Warmblood gelding has had moderate colic for 6 hours. Heart rate is 52 beats/min. On rectal palpation, the taenia of the large colon run from the pelvic inlet dorsally toward the left, ending in the area between the left kidney and the spleen. Transabdominal ultrasound of the left flank can't image the left kidney because of gas shadowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Left dorsal displacement of the large colon (nephrosplenic entrapment)
Right dorsal displacement of the large colon
Large colon volvulus
Ileal impaction
Small colon enterolith

explanation.correct: In nephrosplenic entrapment, the left colon moves dorsally and becomes trapped over the nephrosplenic ligament. On rectal exam, the colonic bands lead toward the nephrosplenic space. On ultrasound, gas in the displaced colon prevents imaging of the left kidney. Treatment options include phenylephrine with exercise, rolling under general anesthesia, or surgery.
options: Classic rectal and ultrasound findings.
In right dorsal displacement the colon lies between the cecum and the right body wall, and bands run cranially across the pelvic inlet on the right.
Volvulus usually causes severe, unrelenting pain, marked distension, and rapid cardiovascular decline.
An impacted ileum is palpated as a firm, tubular structure in the mid-abdomen; the left kidney is still visible on ultrasound.
Enteroliths cause small colon obstruction and usually aren't palpable; the findings described point to left dorsal displacement.
explanation.takeaway: Left kidney can't be seen on ultrasound and colonic bands run to the nephrosplenic space: nephrosplenic entrapment.

reference: Merck Veterinary Manual: Colic in horses (displacement of the large colon)

stem: A 13-year-old overweight pony mare with a cresty neck has had worsening bilateral forelimb lameness for 5 days after turnout on spring pasture. She stands with her weight shifted onto her heels, has bounding digital pulses, and is sensitive to hoof testers at the toe. A lateromedial radiograph of the left front foot is shown (a radiopaque marker is placed on the dorsal hoof wall and a thumbtack marks the apex of the frog). What is the most likely diagnosis?

image.alt: Lateromedial radiograph of an equine front foot with a marker on the dorsal hoof wall
image.credit: Frieda (assumed author; no machine-readable author on source page)

options: Laminitis with rotation of the distal phalanx
Navicular syndrome (palmar foot pain)
Fracture of the distal phalanx
Keratoma
Septic pedal osteitis

explanation.correct: The dorsal surface of the distal phalanx is no longer parallel to the dorsal hoof wall: it has rotated, with the tip pointing toward the sole and the gap between the wall and bone widened. In an obese pony with signs of insulin dysregulation (endocrinopathic laminitis, often triggered by pasture), this means laminitis with rotation. Measure the degree of rotation, distance from the bone to the dorsal wall, and sole depth to guide prognosis and trimming or shoeing. Investigate equine metabolic syndrome and PPID.
options: Rotation of the distal phalanx in the typical clinical setting.
Partly right: also causes bilateral forelimb lameness, but pain localizes to the heel region, and radiographic changes involve the navicular bone, not the alignment of the distal phalanx.
A fracture line would be visible.
A space-occupying lesion in the hoof wall, often causing a focal lucency in the distal phalanx margin.
Septic pedal osteitis causes lysis of the bone margin, usually after a penetrating injury or abscess, not diffuse rotation.
explanation.takeaway: Laminitis on radiographs: the distal phalanx is no longer parallel to the hoof wall. Look for underlying EMS or PPID.

reference: Merck Veterinary Manual: Laminitis in horses; Equine Endocrinology Group recommendations

stem: A 2-year-old Shetland pony at a boarding barn developed a fever of 40.0°C (104°F) a week ago and now has a thick nasal discharge, reduced appetite, and firm, painful swelling between the mandibles. Two other young horses in the barn have similar signs. The pony is shown. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

image.alt: Shetland pony in a stall with bilateral nasal discharge

options: PCR (with culture) for Streptococcus equi subsp. equi on a nasopharyngeal wash or swab, or on pus aspirated from an abscess
Serum SeM antibody titer
PCR for equine herpesvirus-1 on a nasal swab
Transtracheal wash culture
Endoscopic biopsy of the guttural pouch lining

explanation.correct: Fever, mucopurulent nasal discharge and painful submandibular lymphadenopathy in young horses at a shared facility suggest strangles, caused by Streptococcus equi subsp. equi. Confirm with PCR and culture of a nasopharyngeal wash or swab, or of abscess material. Isolate affected horses, monitor temperatures in the rest of the herd, and later screen recovered horses for guttural pouch carriers (endoscopy plus lavage PCR).
options: Confirms the diagnosis.
Partly right: useful for identifying recent exposure and assessing risk of complications such as purpura hemorrhagica or vaccination, but not for confirming acute infection.
EHV-1/4 causes respiratory disease with fever but not abscessing submandibular lymph nodes.
Samples the lower airway; strangles is an upper respiratory and lymph node infection.
Invasive, and not needed for diagnosis. Guttural pouch endoscopy with lavage is used to screen recovered horses for carriers.
explanation.takeaway: Strangles: confirm with PCR and culture of nasopharyngeal or abscess samples, isolate affected horses, and screen guttural pouches for carriers.

reference: ACVIM consensus statement on Streptococcus equi subsp. equi infections in horses (2018)

stem: A 14-year-old pony has had feed material and saliva coming from both nostrils, with repeated attempts to swallow, since eating dry beet pulp 2 hours ago. A firm swelling is palpable on the left side of the neck. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Sedate the pony (e.g., an alpha-2 agonist) so the head lowers, pass a nasogastric tube, and gently lavage the obstruction with water
Give water by oral drench to flush the esophagus
Perform an immediate esophagotomy
Give atropine IV to relax the esophagus
Give mineral oil by oral drench

explanation.correct: Sedation lowers the head, reducing the risk of aspiration, and relaxes the esophagus. Gentle lavage through a nasogastric tube clears most obstructions. Afterward, monitor for aspiration pneumonia and esophageal stricture, and feed soaked food.
options: Standard initial approach.
Oral drenching greatly increases the risk of aspiration.
Reserved for cases that don't respond to medical management.
Atropine can cause ileus and colic in horses and isn't indicated.
Drenching risks aspiration of oil, which causes severe lipid pneumonia.
explanation.takeaway: Choke: sedate so the head lowers, then lavage gently through a nasogastric tube. Watch for aspiration pneumonia.

reference: Merck Veterinary Manual: Esophageal obstruction (choke) in horses

stem: A 7-year-old mare is hospitalized with acute colitis, profuse watery diarrhea, toxic (brick-red) mucous membranes and leukopenia. She isn't lame. Which measure is best supported by evidence to reduce her risk of developing laminitis?
options: Continuous distal limb cryotherapy (e.g., ice boots kept at low temperature)
Hand walking on hard ground several times daily
Corticosteroid therapy at high doses
Hot packing of the hooves
Prophylactic hoof wall resection

explanation.correct: Horses with sepsis or endotoxemia (e.g., colitis, retained placenta, grain overload) are at high risk of laminitis. Continuous digital cryotherapy, cooling the feet to below about 10°C (50°F), has the strongest evidence for prevention in at-risk horses.
options: Best-supported preventive measure.
Exercise on hard ground increases mechanical stress on the laminae.
Corticosteroids are associated with laminitis risk.
Heat increases metabolic demand in the laminae; cooling is protective.
Not a preventive procedure.
explanation.takeaway: Horse with endotoxemia at risk of laminitis: start continuous digital cryotherapy.

reference: Merck Veterinary Manual: Laminitis in horses

stem: A 10-year-old Thoroughbred mare foaled normally 4 hours ago but hasn't passed the fetal membranes. She is bright, afebrile, and nursing her foal. Which initial treatment is most appropriate?
options: Oxytocin IM or IV at low doses, repeated as needed
Forceful manual removal of the membranes
Wait 72 hours before any treatment
Dexamethasone IV
Prostaglandin F2α as the sole treatment after 7 days

explanation.correct: Fetal membranes not passed within 3 hours of foaling are considered retained. Oxytocin is the first-line treatment. The membranes should be tied up so the mare doesn't step on them. Forceful traction risks hemorrhage, leaving tissue behind, and uterine damage. Untreated retention can lead to metritis, endotoxemia and laminitis.
options: First-line treatment.
Risks uterine damage and incomplete removal.
Delay risks metritis, endotoxemia and laminitis.
Corticosteroids aren't indicated and may increase laminitis risk.
Too late, and not first-line.
explanation.takeaway: Membranes retained more than 3 hours after foaling: give oxytocin and monitor for metritis and laminitis.

reference: Merck Veterinary Manual: Retained fetal membranes in mares

stem: You are called to a remote trail where a horse has an open, comminuted fracture of the radius and must be euthanized immediately. Barbiturates aren't available. According to AVMA euthanasia guidelines, which method is acceptable with conditions?
options: A properly placed gunshot or penetrating captive bolt applied by a trained person
IV potassium chloride in the conscious horse
Succinylcholine IV as the sole agent
Exsanguination of the conscious horse
IV air injection in the conscious horse

explanation.correct: For horses, AVMA lists gunshot and penetrating captive bolt (correctly placed by trained personnel) as acceptable with conditions. Potassium chloride, exsanguination and air embolism are acceptable only in an animal already under general anesthesia. Neuromuscular blockers used alone are unacceptable.
options: Acceptable with conditions.
Acceptable only after general anesthesia.
Paralysis without unconsciousness is unacceptable.
Only acceptable in an unconscious animal.
Only acceptable in an anesthetized animal.
explanation.takeaway: Know which euthanasia methods are acceptable and which are acceptable only under general anesthesia.

reference: AVMA Guidelines for the Euthanasia of Animals (2020): Equids

stem: A new horse owner asks which vaccines every horse in North America should receive, regardless of use or location. Which answer reflects the AAEP core vaccines?
options: Tetanus, Eastern and Western equine encephalomyelitis, West Nile virus, and rabies
Strangles, influenza, and equine herpesvirus only
Tetanus and Potomac horse fever only
Rabies and botulism only
No vaccines are recommended for every horse

explanation.correct: AAEP core vaccines are tetanus, EEE/WEE, West Nile virus and rabies: diseases that are endemic, a risk to every horse, severe, or of public-health importance. Risk-based vaccines (e.g., influenza, EHV, strangles, Potomac horse fever, botulism) depend on the horse's exposure.
options: AAEP core vaccines.
These are risk-based vaccines.
Incomplete, and Potomac horse fever is risk-based.
Incomplete, and botulism is risk-based.
Incorrect.
explanation.takeaway: AAEP core vaccines: tetanus, EEE/WEE, West Nile virus and rabies.

stem: You need to examine the left hind limb of a nervous horse held by a handler. Which positioning is safest for the handler and the examiner?
options: Handler and examiner stand on the same side of the horse, so the horse's hindquarters swing away from both if it moves
Handler on the right side and examiner on the left side
Examiner stands directly behind the horse to observe the limb
Examiner kneels beside the hind limb for a closer view
Horse tied to a fixed object with no handler

explanation.correct: If the handler and examiner are on the same side, pulling the head toward that side swings the hindquarters away from both people. Staying close to the horse's body, never kneeling or sitting, and not standing directly behind it reduces the risk of injury.
options: Same-side positioning.
Opposite-side positioning means turning the head pushes the hindquarters toward one person.
In the kick zone.
Kneeling prevents a quick escape.
A tied, nervous horse may panic and pull back.
explanation.takeaway: Horse restraint: handler and examiner on the same side, and never kneel.

reference: Merck Veterinary Manual: Restraint of horses

stem: A 7-year-old Thoroughbred gelding has developed asymmetric ataxia and weakness over 3 weeks. There is gluteal muscle atrophy on the left side. He lives on a farm in Kentucky where opossums are often seen. Which test result most supports equine protozoal myeloencephalitis?
options: Low serum:CSF anti-Sarcocystis neurona antibody ratio
A positive serum antibody test for Sarcocystis neurona alone
Increased creatine kinase and AST on serum chemistry
Narrowed vertebral canal on standing lateral cervical radiographs
Positive PCR for equine herpesvirus 1 on a nasal swab

explanation.correct: EPM is caused by Sarcocystis neurona, with the opossum as definitive host. Asymmetric ataxia with focal muscle atrophy is typical. Many horses in endemic areas are seropositive without disease, so a positive serum test alone means only exposure. Comparing paired serum and CSF antibody levels (serum:CSF titer ratio or antibody index) shows intrathecal antibody production and is the most useful test.
options: Correct. A low serum:CSF ratio indicates antibody made within the CNS.
Seroprevalence in endemic areas is high, so serum alone does not confirm EPM.
CK and AST rise with muscle disease, not EPM.
Cervical canal narrowing suggests cervical vertebral compressive myelopathy, which is usually symmetric.
EHV-1 myeloencephalopathy usually causes sudden, symmetric hind limb signs with urine dribbling.
explanation.takeaway: Confirm EPM with paired serum and CSF antibody testing; serum alone shows only exposure.

reference: Reed SM et al., ACVIM consensus statement on EPM (J Vet Intern Med 2016)

stem: A 10-year-old Quarter Horse gelding has a gradual-onset lameness in both forelimbs, worse on the right. The lameness is worse when circling on a hard surface and improves on soft ground. Hoof testers produce a consistent response over the middle third of the frog. Which diagnostic finding best localizes the source of pain?
options: Lameness resolves after a palmar digital block, then appears in the left forelimb
Lameness improves markedly after intra-articular anesthesia of the fetlock joint
A positive response to an upper limb flexion test
Heat, pain and swelling over the superficial digital flexor tendon in the mid-metacarpus
Lameness is unchanged after bilateral abaxial sesamoid nerve blocks

explanation.correct: Bilateral forelimb lameness worse on circles on hard ground, with frog sensitivity, is typical of navicular syndrome (palmar foot pain). A palmar digital nerve block desensitizes the palmar part of the foot. If the lameness resolves and then appears in the other forelimb, the pain is bilateral and in the palmar foot.
options: Correct. Switching lameness after a palmar digital block shows bilateral palmar foot pain.
Fetlock blocks do not reach the palmar foot.
Flexion tests are not specific and do not localize pain to the navicular region.
These signs point to tendinitis, not palmar foot pain.
An abaxial sesamoid block desensitizes the whole foot; no improvement would argue against foot pain.
explanation.takeaway: Palmar digital nerve blocks localize palmar foot pain; a lameness that switches limbs suggests bilateral disease.

reference: Baxter GM, Adams and Stashak's Lameness in Horses
